bodyText:
I counted my dog photos.

I have 1,247 photos of my dog on my phone. He is four years old. That's roughly one photo of him every single day for his entire life.
I have done nothing with any of them.

I bought him a custom portrait once. It sat in a closet. I bought a custom mug with his face on it. I broke it in the dishwasher. I follow approximately eleven other dogs on Instagram and every one of them has a more curated digital presence than my actual real-life dog.

So I tried something different.

I picked twelve of my favorite photos of him — him as a puppy, him sleeping with his tongue out, him on the beach, him with his stupid tennis ball, him on the couch giving me the side-eye I love — and I uploaded them.

A week later a real printed colouring book showed up. Every page was him.

I cannot describe how funny it was to open. Twelve pages of my dog. As outlines. As a colouring book. Like a children's book starring my idiot golden retriever.

I started colouring it that night. I did three pages. He sat next to me on the couch the entire time, completely unaware that the literal book in my lap was about him.

I love this book more than I should. It's funny and it's stupid and it's also genuinely the only physical record I have of him at this stage of his life.

If you have eight hundred photos of your dog — finally do something with them.
title: 1,247 Photos of My Dog. Finally Worth It.
linkDescription: A custom colouring book made from your real pet photos.

bodyText:
🔥 At 25 weeks pregnant, I caught my husband cheating. Then he said we'd divorce after our daughter was born. I said yes, took the Stanford offer, and chose myself. 
Chapter 1 What Is the Gender?
Twenty-five weeks pregnant, Sloane Powell caught her husband cheating—right outside the hospital.

A tall, striking man in a black overcoat was shielding a soft, delicate-looking girl in his arms. The girl wore a white fox-fur coat. Her cheeks were rosy, her small face tucked into a fluffy wool scarf, her features pretty as a porcelain doll.

Sloane clenched her prenatal checkup slip so hard her fingers went white. The cold wind sliced across her face, but it was nothing compared to the stabbing ache in her chest.

Jaxson Cole saw her from far away. His expression stayed indifferent, not a trace of shame at being caught. He personally opened the car door for the girl, his demeanor gentle.

So the cold, untouchable man at the top of the world could be tender, too.

The girl seemed to notice Sloane. She paused, looked at Sloane with confusion first, then turned to Jaxson and asked, “Why is that old woman staring at you? Jaxson, do you know her?”

The wind howled in Sloane’s ears.

She didn’t know what else the girl said to Jaxson.

But from the shape of her mouth, Sloane could clearly make out two words.

“Old woman.”

That was supposed to be her.

Sloane’s lips curled into a bitter smile.

She was only twenty-four.

But she’d always been a little chubby, with an ordinary face. Wrapped in a black puffer jacket and a black knit hat, her late-pregnancy body was swollen and heavy. Add in the exhaustion on her face, and she really did look like some worn-out woman in her thirties or forties—how could she compare to a young, bright, beautiful girl?

Jaxson protected the girl as she got into the car.

Sloane stood frozen, watching the vehicle pull away.

She and Jaxson had married because of the baby. This forced marriage—to a man like Jaxson, heaven’s chosen—was a stain on his life. The child in her belly was the tool she’d used to corner him.

He hated her.

And she had loved him in secret for eight years.

Sloane knew she never deserved him. All she could do was study harder, keep pushing, take him as her life’s ideal, and chase after his footsteps.

Finally, she got what she wanted. She became his assistant. She could stand close to him.

But that night destroyed more than Jaxson.

It also tore apart every last shred of pride and dignity she’d ever had in front of him.

She would never forget the way he’d stared at her afterward—disgusted, like he’d touched something filthy that made him sick.

So, of course, only a beautiful girl like that deserved him.

A hot tear slid from the corner of her eye. Then her lower abdomen cramped hard. She hurriedly held her belly with one hand and braced the stone pillar beside her with the other.

A passing nurse saw her and rushed over, supporting her and taking her into an exam room.

It was just the emotional shock—she’d stirred the baby.

Once she calmed down…

Sloane left the hospital, driving alone back to Emerald Bay Mansion with a body and soul that felt wrung dry.

This was Jaxson’s villa.

Wren Cole, Jaxson’s grandmother, had arranged for experienced housekeepers from the Cole Estate to look after her.

At that moment, the two housekeepers assigned to her were sitting in the warm living room like they owned the place, eating good food and laughing together.

When they heard the sound, they turned toward the door.

Seeing Sloane back, one of them stood and walked over, asking, “How were the results?”

The attitude was arrogant, the tone dripping with contempt.

They were supposed to be taking care of her, but they looked more like they were here to watch her and act like the real masters.

Sloane only gave the housekeeper a cold glance and didn’t answer, heading straight for the stairs.

The housekeeper frowned in displeasure.

“I’m talking to you.”

Sloane still ignored her.

Only then did Wren’s attitude toward Sloane soften.

But everyone else in the Cole family still looked down on her.

A girl.

Mrs. Cole’s side had probably already gotten the hospital’s notice.

When she didn’t answer, Leo continued, “If you’re not available—”

“Professor Grant,” Sloane said.

Leo replied, “Come by my office tomorrow at ten.”

“Okay.”

Sloane set the phone down and let out a long breath. For the first time in a while, it felt like the clouds had parted, letting a sliver of moonlight through.

A man who didn’t love you—no matter what you gave him, no matter if you bore his child—would never stay. He wouldn’t even glance back.

Her phone rang again. This time it was Wren, asking her to come back to the Cole Estate. Sloane agreed. It was probably about the baby.

She went to the bathroom and took a long, hot shower.

How could someone like her ever deserve to stand next to Jaxson?

But the moment she stepped outside, Jaxson called. His voice came through flat and cold. “Come out.”

Sloane startled.

Wren must’ve told him to come back too.

She answered, “Okay.”

Outside the villa, his Rolls-Royce sat idling at the entrance.

Two hours ago, that same car had picked up another woman and dropped her off somewhere.

Sloane took a deep breath, walked over, opened the door, and got in.

The moment she sat down, she caught a faint scent—sweet and young. On the seat beside her sat a pink teddy bear, the kind of plushie a girl would adore.

When she lifted her gaze, she noticed a hair tie wrapped around the man’s wrist.

A quiet claim.

Jaxson must really like that girl.

Sloane swallowed the sour ache rising in her chest, sat up straight, and buckled her seatbelt.

The driver pulled away smoothly.

Sloane stared out the window, silent.

Because she’d foolishly convinced herself they were already husband and wife—that they had a child, that there was a long future ahead. If she became a good wife, a good mother… maybe one day Jaxson would finally turn and see her.

Sloane answered, “A girl.”

The words landed.

Sloane’s fingers tightened.

It felt like a hand had clenched around her heart, making it hard to breathe.

This marriage was never meant to last. She’d always known. But hearing him say it—now, like this—still cut deeper than she’d expected.

She bit her lip and answered, “Okay.”

Jaxson turned his head to glance at her, as if surprised she’d agreed so easily.

Chapter 2 He Came Home Early
But he didn’t dig into it any further.

Night.

“You…”

He was flipping through documents in his hand, his features hard and cold, his whole body giving off a distant, untouchable chill.

Even if he came back, they still slept separately.

He slept in the master bedroom on the second floor.

She slept in the guest room on the first.

The next day.

Because Jaxson was home, the housekeeper prepared a lavish breakfast.

He sat at the main seat and didn’t see Sloane.

Sloane was surprised.

Only pregnant?

Yeah.

To him, this accidental child probably meant nothing at all.

This sudden scolding of his had to be because Maren had been running her mouth to him.

And it wasn’t the first time.

Sloane stirred the porridge in her bowl, her voice even. “If they resent having to look after me, then send them back to the main house. I can manage on my own.”

Jaxson’s brows drew together.

Sloane recognized that expression—it was his tell. Displeasure.

“I’m telling you. I’m not asking for your input.”

Sloane lowered her head and fell silent.

Jaxson looked at her—that flat, hollow expression—and his jaw tightened.

Sloane’s fingers tightened around her fork.

Breakfast ended.

Jaxson left.

Sloane went to Silverlake University.

She arrived at Leo’s office.

Sloane raised her hand and knocked.

“Professor Grant.”

Only a beautiful, stunning woman was worthy of him.

And she’d taken the day off anyway.

That night.

The next day.

"Mr. Cole."

The man walked past as if she weren't there and strode into the building.

At two in the afternoon.

Then.

The moment she left the office.

As she spoke.

Back at her workstation.

Watching her father grow older and more worn by the day—so desperate he was already selling off assets just to pay debts—Sloane finally made her choice and went to the Cole family. Back then, she’d had her own selfish reasons. It wasn’t only for her father. It was for herself, too.

She did get what she wanted. The Powell family cleared the debt because of a huge bride price from the Cole family.

But she’d paid the price she was supposed to pay.

So the pain she suffered now… it was all her own doing. She couldn’t blame anyone else.

Back at the Powell House.

Nora came out of the kitchen. “Sloane, you’re back.”

When Sloane was nine, her mother divorced her father. Her mother took her brother and left Sloane behind.

Later, Nora met her father, but the two of them never got a marriage license. They lived together like partners.

At first, Sloane didn’t accept her—she even hated her. But little by little, she felt Nora’s kindness. And Ezra treated her so well. After losing her brother, she’d gained a new one.

“Aunt Nora, where are my dad and them?”

“They should be on the way. They’ll be back soon. Go rest for a bit first.”

“Okay.”

Sloane went back to her room. Even though she was married, her father had always kept a bedroom for her, renovated in the style she liked.

Back in a place that belonged to her, all the exhaustion and bitterness inside her vanished in a single breath.

She sat on the edge of the bed and saw the photo album on the nightstand. She reached for it and opened it. The very first photo was a torn family portrait.

The picture was old.

She had been eight that year.

Her young, handsome father held her in his arms. Beside him stood her brother—he’d been fourteen. On the other side was her mother.

She was the one who had ripped the photo.

Because she’d hated her mother for taking her brother and abandoning her and her dad. Time had passed, and now that ripping, splitting pain no longer existed the way it used to.

She turned to the next page.

In the photo, a teenage girl looked bright and beautiful. She wore a long white dress and a light-brown woven little square cap, standing beneath golden ginkgo trees. The sunlight fell perfectly over the girl’s radiant smile.

Long black hair. A small oval face. Features that were vivid and striking, moonlit and mesmerizing. Especially those eyes—sparkling like stars in the sky.

But later, she’d gotten seriously ill and had to take steroid medication. Her body slowly gained weight. No matter how she tried to lose it, nothing worked. She could only rely on starvation and exercise to keep herself from getting even bigger.

All at once, Sloane thought of the girl from today.

Her features looked somewhat like the girl in this photo—especially those eyes.

Chapter 6 Far Out of Her League
Knock, knock, knock.
"Sloane, your dad and brother are back," Nora called through the door after knocking.

Sloane didn't think much of it. She set the photo album down, got up, and walked out. The moment she saw the two men coming in, her face lit up. "Dad, Ezra."

Ezra and Silas Powell both looked at her.

"Sloane, I brought you something. Come see if you like it," Ezra said, motioning her over.

Sloane hurried toward him, delighted. "What is it?"

Ezra carried in several bags and set them on the coffee table. Then he pulled out a designer jewelry box and handed it to her. "Open it."

Sloane took it happily. Inside lay a beautifully crafted gold bracelet. "Thank you, Ezra. I love it."

"Glad you like it."

Ezra reached out and ruffled Sloane's hair with easy affection.

He'd also bought Nora a different gold bracelet that suited her, along with skincare sets for both women. For Silas, he brought tea and liquor, plus local specialties.

The atmosphere was warm, easy—the way home should feel.

Only here did Sloane feel like she could finally breathe.

"Sloane, when are you due?" Ezra asked, concern creeping into his voice.

Her belly really did look like someone else's late-term pregnancy.

"Two more months," Sloane answered.

"Sloane must be carrying a girl," Nora said with a smile.

Sloane nodded. "It is a girl."

"You checked?" Silas asked.

Nora seemed to catch something and tensed up alongside him.

"Yeah. But Wren cares a lot about this baby," Sloane said.

Silas finally let out a breath. "Good. As long as there's a child, you and Jaxson will slowly work things out down the road."

Sloane lowered her eyes. Her chest tightened, heavy and aching, and for a moment she didn't know how to respond. Jaxson had already brought up divorce.

But she couldn't hide it forever.

And she'd already decided to move out of Emerald Bay Mansion and come home.

Forget it. She'd tell them after dinner.

Nora prepared an elaborate meal.

Ezra had partnered with a friend to start a tech company. Two years ago, when the business was just getting off the ground, Silas hadn't hesitated—he'd given Ezra startup capital. The company was doing extremely well now, focusing mainly on AI. This trip had been for a partnership deal, and it had gone smoothly.

Silas, meanwhile, was in the process of selling off his own company.

Before, thanks to the bride price from the Cole family, the company had managed to stay afloat. But the economy was struggling now, and pivoting had proven nearly impossible. The business simply couldn't survive.

He was getting older, with far less energy than before. He believed strongly in Ezra's company. Ezra's company would enter its financing stage by the end of the year, so it was the perfect time to sell his own business and invest everything into Ezra's.

Then he shared another piece of good news: Silas was going to officially get the marriage license with Nora.

Nora's eyes immediately welled up.

Years of standing by his side had finally led to this.

Sloane had no objections. She knew her father had held back all these years because, deep down, he still missed her mother.

She'd never understood why her mother had divorced and left a man as good as him.

But now it didn't matter.

On a day like this—

She couldn't bear to ruin the mood.

But in the end, she still said it.

“Dad. Aunt Nora. Ezra.” She forced the words out. “Jaxson is planning to divorce me.”

The moment it left her mouth, the dining room went dead silent.

Everyone’s expression turned heavy, especially Silas. He lowered his head, his face tight.

The result wasn’t exactly a shock.

Only the speed of it was.

The Powell family and the Cole family had become in-laws, but there had been no wedding—just a marriage certificate. In the past six months, the two families had had no contact at all.

Jaxson had never once stepped into the Powell family home.

No matter the holidays, the Cole side never sent gifts.

Every time Sloane came home alone, Silas and Nora would prepare holiday gifts and have her deliver them to the Cole family.

When she brought them over, Wren would accept them politely, but Sloane knew she handed them straight to the staff at Cole Estate.

Lyra, on the other hand, had a servant throw them directly into the trash right in front of Sloane, telling her not to let her family send that kind of low-class junk again.

Jaxson only reminded her not to do something so pointless.

In a marriage that unequal, going their separate ways had always been a matter of time.

Sloane pressed her lips together and continued, “But we’ll wait until after the baby is born. And I already agreed to Professor Grant—I’m going to Stanford University for advanced study next February.”

Ezra was the first to break the suffocating silence. “Going for advanced study is good. Sloane, you’re so outstanding. You shouldn’t be trapped in a marriage. No matter what you decide, I’m backing you.”

Sloane smiled and nodded. “Thanks, Ezra.”

Silas sighed—a sigh full of endless helplessness and guilt. “Then divorce. It’s all Dad’s fault. People like us… ordinary folks… we really can’t reach a family like the Coles.”

Sloane’s eyes burned red. All the pain she’d endured lately suddenly felt small compared to this.

She had her family.

They were her shield, her support.

With them behind her, there was no hurdle she couldn’t get over.

Seeing her like that, Nora quickly grabbed a tissue and wiped at Sloane’s reddened eyes, soothing her.

In the end, the family still finished this dinner with smiles.

At the same time.

In the southern suburbs, at Cloud Peak One—an area that had existed for over twenty years, an old-money neighborhood with aging infrastructure.

A Bentley slowly stopped at the gate of Villa 12.

This villa was the one the Powell family had sold.

The car window slid down, revealing a handsome, flawless profile. He looked into the villa. Inside, the lights were blazing.

Warm yellow streetlight fell into his eyes, unable to hide the complexity and loneliness there.

He pulled his gaze back and lit a cigarette.

Then his phone vibrated.

He picked up and answered, his voice gentle. “What’s wrong, Liora?”

Liora’s sweetly complaining voice came through. “Declan, when are you getting here? I’m starving. And Jaxson won’t even let me eat first.”

Right after that, a low, indulgent male voice sounded on the other end. “Who was it that told me to remind her to watch her mouth? Now she’s blaming me?”

Liora huffed.

“If you’re hungry, eat first. I’ll be there soon,” he said.

He hung up.

Declan stubbed out the cigarette. Then, one last time, he looked out the window.

He raised the window and drove away from the villa.

bodyText:
For Tacoma, his best friend Chris Carson , and anyone who has had to say goodbye to a piece of their heart. 🕊️
Some dogs don't just share our lives. They hold them together.

Tacoma was a service dog, a fierce fighter, and Chris’s loyal companion for over a decade. When a devastating cancer diagnosis arrived, Tacoma didn't just decline quietly—he fought through major surgeries, chemotherapy, radiation, and even emergency bloat surgery.

On January 1st, vets gave him mere days to live. Tacoma gave them five more beautiful months.

Even in his final weeks, he was still eating, still wagging his tail, and still completely happy. He felt good until the very end, finally letting Chris know on his last weekend that he was tired and it was time. On June 1st, 2026, he passed away peacefully.

We had the profound privilege of working with Chris on Tacoma’s custom portrait for over a month before he passed. Getting to know them, hearing about Tacoma’s daily victories, and witnessing their unbreakable bond in those final weeks deeply moved us.

We wanted to share their incredible journey to honor a dog who truly changed what we believe is possible.

📖 The link to read Tacoma's full story is in the comments below.

If you have a faithful companion like Tacoma, our inbox is always open. We would love to hear their story at bella@pembertonportraits.com.

Rest easy, Tacoma. You did your job beautifully. 🐾

bodyText:
🔥 At 25 weeks pregnant, I caught my husband cheating. Then he said we'd divorce after our daughter was born. I said yes, took the Stanford offer, and chose myself. 
Chapter 1 What Is the Gender?
Twenty-five weeks pregnant, Sloane Powell caught her husband cheating—right outside the hospital.

A tall, striking man in a black overcoat was shielding a soft, delicate-looking girl in his arms. The girl wore a white fox-fur coat. Her cheeks were rosy, her small face tucked into a fluffy wool scarf, her features pretty as a porcelain doll.

Sloane clenched her prenatal checkup slip so hard her fingers went white. The cold wind sliced across her face, but it was nothing compared to the stabbing ache in her chest.

Jaxson Cole saw her from far away. His expression stayed indifferent, not a trace of shame at being caught. He personally opened the car door for the girl, his demeanor gentle.

So the cold, untouchable man at the top of the world could be tender, too.

The girl seemed to notice Sloane. She paused, looked at Sloane with confusion first, then turned to Jaxson and asked, “Why is that old woman staring at you? Jaxson, do you know her?”

The wind howled in Sloane’s ears.

She didn’t know what else the girl said to Jaxson.

But from the shape of her mouth, Sloane could clearly make out two words.

“Old woman.”

That was supposed to be her.

Sloane’s lips curled into a bitter smile.

She was only twenty-four.

But she’d always been a little chubby, with an ordinary face. Wrapped in a black puffer jacket and a black knit hat, her late-pregnancy body was swollen and heavy. Add in the exhaustion on her face, and she really did look like some worn-out woman in her thirties or forties—how could she compare to a young, bright, beautiful girl?

Jaxson protected the girl as she got into the car.

Sloane stood frozen, watching the vehicle pull away.

She and Jaxson had married because of the baby. This forced marriage—to a man like Jaxson, heaven’s chosen—was a stain on his life. The child in her belly was the tool she’d used to corner him.

He hated her.

And she had loved him in secret for eight years.

Sloane knew she never deserved him. All she could do was study harder, keep pushing, take him as her life’s ideal, and chase after his footsteps.

Finally, she got what she wanted. She became his assistant. She could stand close to him.

But that night destroyed more than Jaxson.

It also tore apart every last shred of pride and dignity she’d ever had in front of him.

She would never forget the way he’d stared at her afterward—disgusted, like he’d touched something filthy that made him sick.

So, of course, only a beautiful girl like that deserved him.

A hot tear slid from the corner of her eye. Then her lower abdomen cramped hard. She hurriedly held her belly with one hand and braced the stone pillar beside her with the other.

A passing nurse saw her and rushed over, supporting her and taking her into an exam room.

It was just the emotional shock—she’d stirred the baby.

Once she calmed down…

Sloane left the hospital, driving alone back to Emerald Bay Mansion with a body and soul that felt wrung dry.

This was Jaxson’s villa.

Wren Cole, Jaxson’s grandmother, had arranged for experienced housekeepers from the Cole Estate to look after her.

At that moment, the two housekeepers assigned to her were sitting in the warm living room like they owned the place, eating good food and laughing together.

When they heard the sound, they turned toward the door.

Seeing Sloane back, one of them stood and walked over, asking, “How were the results?”

The attitude was arrogant, the tone dripping with contempt.

They were supposed to be taking care of her, but they looked more like they were here to watch her and act like the real masters.

Sloane only gave the housekeeper a cold glance and didn’t answer, heading straight for the stairs.

The housekeeper frowned in displeasure.

“I’m talking to you.”

Sloane still ignored her.

The housekeeper spat toward Sloane’s back. “Fat as a pig. You really think you’re some young mistress of the Cole family? Who are you trying to fool?”

Back in her bedroom, Sloane sat on the bed, hollow and lost.

Neither Jaxson nor the Cole family had ever accepted her.

Wren had been the one to make the decision and force her and Jaxson to get their marriage certificate.

But that was only because Noah Cole, Jaxson’s grandfather, had been critically ill. She’d shown up pregnant at just the right time, and they’d arranged the marriage to bring him good luck—two happy events at once.

Whether it was coincidence or whether the “good luck” was real, Noah’s condition gradually improved.

Only then did Wren’s attitude toward Sloane soften.

But everyone else in the Cole family still looked down on her.

Today’s hospital visit had been to confirm the baby’s gender.

A girl.

Mrs. Cole’s side had probably already gotten the hospital’s notice.

Just then, her phone vibrated.

Sloane pulled herself out of her thoughts.

She reached into her bag and pulled out her phone. When she saw the caller ID, she froze—it was her advisor.

She picked up.

“Professor Grant.”

“A spot just opened up for advanced study at Stanford—PhD track. You interested?”

At Leo Grant’s words, Sloane went still for a long moment.

When she didn’t answer, Leo continued, “If you’re not available—”

“I’m in.”

Sloane snapped back to the moment and answered with quiet certainty.

This time, Leo fell silent.

He knew better than anyone how hard Sloane had fought just to be worthy of standing beside Jaxson.

Now that she finally had what she wanted—marriage, a baby on the way—how could she possibly walk away?

He’d only mentioned the last slot on a whim, testing the waters.

“Professor Grant,” Sloane said.

Leo replied, “Come by my office tomorrow at ten.”

“Okay.”

He hung up without another word.

Sloane set the phone down and let out a long breath. For the first time in a while, it felt like the clouds had parted, letting a sliver of moonlight through.

She needed to wake up.

A man who didn’t love you—no matter what you gave him, no matter if you bore his child—would never stay. He wouldn’t even glance back.

Her phone rang again. This time it was Wren, asking her to come back to the Cole Estate. Sloane agreed. It was probably about the baby.

Now she finally had a bit of energy.

She went to the bathroom and took a long, hot shower.

Afterward, sitting at the vanity, Sloane studied herself in the mirror—puffy face, dark circles under her eyes, sunken eyelids, cheeks dotted with freckles.

Looking this worn down… who wouldn’t be repulsed?

How could someone like her ever deserve to stand next to Jaxson?

She put on makeup, slipped into a pink puffer jacket, and pulled on a white beanie. She looked much more presentable.

She’d planned to drive herself back to the main residence.

But the moment she stepped outside, Jaxson called. His voice came through flat and cold. “Come out.”

Sloane startled.

Wren must’ve told him to come back too.

She answered, “Okay.”

Outside the villa, his Rolls-Royce sat idling at the entrance.

Two hours ago, that same car had picked up another woman and dropped her off somewhere.

Sloane took a deep breath, walked over, opened the door, and got in.

The moment she sat down, she caught a faint scent—sweet and young. On the seat beside her sat a pink teddy bear, the kind of plushie a girl would adore.

When she lifted her gaze, she noticed a hair tie wrapped around the man’s wrist.

A quiet claim.

Jaxson must really like that girl.

Sloane swallowed the sour ache rising in her chest, sat up straight, and buckled her seatbelt.

The driver pulled away smoothly.

Sloane stared out the window, silent.

Before, every moment alone with him had been something to treasure. She’d inch closer, start conversations over and over, even if he looked down on her.

Because she’d foolishly convinced herself they were already husband and wife—that they had a child, that there was a long future ahead. If she became a good wife, a good mother… maybe one day Jaxson would finally turn and see her.

But in the end, it had all been lies she told herself.

The man didn’t care about her feelings. As always, he was detached, asking in a casual tone, “What’s the baby’s gender?”

Sloane answered, “A girl.”

Hearing that, nothing shifted in Jaxson’s sharp, handsome features. He only said flatly, “After the baby’s born, we’ll get divorced.”

The words landed.

Sloane’s fingers tightened.

It felt like a hand had clenched around her heart, making it hard to breathe.

This marriage was never meant to last. She’d always known. But hearing him say it—now, like this—still cut deeper than she’d expected.

She bit her lip and answered, “Okay.”

Jaxson turned his head to glance at her, as if surprised she’d agreed so easily.

Chapter 2 He Came Home Early
But he didn’t dig into it any further.

Sloane followed up right away. “Tomorrow’s Monday. Do you have time in the afternoon? Why don’t we go to Civil Council early and get it handled? It shouldn’t matter if we do it two months ahead of time, right?”

Even after signing, there was still a one-month cooling-off period. And it wouldn’t be long before she gave birth.

Jaxson looked at her. She was too calm, too straightforward. Something like scrutiny flickered in his eyes before he pulled his gaze back. “Whenever I call, that’s the time.”

Sloane lowered her eyes and didn’t speak again.

The car arrived at the Cole Estate.

Wren had called them back because of the baby in Sloane’s belly.

The Cole family had more men than women.

Wren had two sons. The eldest was Ethan Cole. The younger was Julian Cole.

Ethan had two sons. The eldest, Felix Cole, had gotten married a few years ago and had a pair of twin boys. They were five this year. The younger, Miles Cole, was twenty-four and still unmarried.

Julian only had one son—Jaxson.

So when it turned out Sloane was carrying a girl, both Wren and Noah were overjoyed.

“It really is good news. The moment our little sweetheart arrives, the old man’s illness is basically cured.”

Seeing how much her mother-in-law valued the baby, Lyra quickly echoed her, then added a couple of nice words to Sloane.

Sloane sat quietly to the side, hands folded, her posture obedient.

Looking at her—plump, head bowed, meek as could be—Lyra found her hard to stomach. But with Wren right there, she kept it off her face.

Wren, however, was in high spirits. She gifted Sloane an expensive emerald bracelet.

Sloane blinked, flustered, and immediately tried to refuse, pushing it gently back.

Lyra Cole, Jaxson’s mother, spoke up. “If Wren’s giving it to you, take it.”

So small-town. So timid. Just like someone who’d never learned how to carry herself in public.

Sloane stopped protesting and accepted the bracelet. “Thank you, Grandma.”

“Take good care of that baby. Give us a healthy, chubby little one.”

Sloane smiled and nodded. She knew Wren’s kindness had nothing to do with her.

Originally, she and Jaxson were supposed to stay for dinner.

Until Jaxson stepped out to take a call.

Through the glass door, she saw something shift in his expression—a softness in his eyes, indulgent, almost tender.

It sounded like they’d just gotten a pet.

Jaxson murmured the pet’s name. Sweetie.

If he married the woman he actually loved, she thought, he’d probably make a good father.

“Mm. I’ll be right there.”

He hung up.

When Jaxson turned and walked back in from the balcony, he found Sloane standing just inside. She flinched, slow to react, lifting her gaze to meet his—only to be met with the cold, distant face of a stranger.

Her chest tightened. She managed, “Grandma wants you in the study.”

He said nothing. Just walked past her.

Sloane stayed where she was, heart clenched in a grip she couldn’t loosen.

She didn’t know how long she stood there before she finally came back to herself.

Jaxson reached the study.

Wren and Noah were both inside.

“Jaxson,” Wren began, “Grandma knows you don’t have feelings for Sloane. But the baby’s almost here. And Sloane herself is accomplished—top university, well-educated, gentle. What this marriage needs right now is stability. She’s the most suitable partner for raising children and supporting her husband.”

Jaxson said nothing.

But the faint furrow in his brow—the tension there—spoke volumes.

How could Wren not see it? Sloane really was plain. Standing next to her grandson, they just didn’t look right together.

Noah cut in. “Right now, your marriage can’t afford any disruptions. If you truly don’t care for her, as long as she doesn’t do anything reckless, keep things steady for a year or two.”

Wren added, “Exactly. Too many people are watching you, waiting for a story. Let her raise the child first. Divorce later—it won’t be too late.”

Jaxson was quiet for a long moment. His handsome features revealed nothing. Finally, he said, “Grandpa, Grandma. I understand.”

When Sloane saw Wren again later, Wren said simply, “Something came up at Jaxson’s office. He had to leave. I’ll have the driver take you home.”

Sloane nodded. “Okay.”

Before she left that day, Wren reminded her, “Even though you’re pregnant, you still need to exercise more and take care of yourself. Back when Lyra was pregnant, she still had to accompany her husband to events and manage the household. Some things are easy to get, but holding onto them isn’t easy.”

Sloane understood instantly what Wren meant.

Being a daughter-in-law in  Cole family wasn’t easy. If she wanted to secure her position, she had to change herself.

And in her current state, she would only embarrass Jaxson.

She had thought about getting better—working out, doing yoga, trying to lose weight. But she lacked the drive to keep going. She grew exhausted in body and mind, and her weight only climbed.

But Wren was right. She couldn’t keep sinking like this—though not to secure her place. For her future self.

“Grandma, I understand.”

Night.

What surprised Sloane was that the man who’d brought up divorce that morning actually came home.

“You…”

“Make me a bowl of chicken soup and bring it to the study.”

After that, Jaxson went upstairs to the study.

Sloane snapped back to herself, went to the kitchen, cooked a bowl of chicken soup, and delivered it to the study.

He was flipping through documents in his hand, his features hard and cold, his whole body giving off a distant, untouchable chill.

She didn’t disturb him. She turned and left the study.

Even if he came back, they still slept separately.

He slept in the master bedroom on the second floor.

She slept in the guest room on the first.

The next day.

Because Jaxson was home, the housekeeper prepared a lavish breakfast.

He sat at the main seat and didn’t see Sloane.

Usually, when he was home, Sloane not only ironed and prepared the clothes he’d wear the next day, she also made his breakfast herself. She really had been a dutiful, proper wife.

But that morning, there were no freshly ironed clothes laid out. And breakfast had been made by the kitchen staff.

“Where is she?” Jaxson asked, irritation creeping into his voice.

Maren didn’t hesitate to unload her grievances. “I went to wake her first thing, and she just refuses to get out of bed. Every day we have to bring meals to her room. She acts like we don’t exist. Ask her what she wants to eat—she won’t say a word. We’re not mind readers. She’s just pregnant, that’s all. When Mrs. Cole was expecting you, Sir, she still serve Mr. Cole well. But this one? She acts like she’s checked into a resort.”

Jaxson’s brow tightened. “Go wake her up.”

“Yes, sir.”

Sloane had actually been awake for a while. She was just waiting for Jaxson to leave.

Then the door swung open, and Maren walked in without knocking. Spotting Sloane already seated on the sofa, she let out a sneer thick with contempt. “Oh, look at that. The Young Madam, waiting to be invited out of bed.”

Sloane lifted her gaze, her voice cool. “I’m not. Are you?”

For months, Sloane had kept her head down, never once talked back.

Maren hadn’t expected that.

“If you keep forgetting your place, don’t blame me if I tell Wren exactly how you’ve been carrying on.”

She was getting divorced anyway. What did she have to lose? With two months left, why keep swallowing insults?

Maren’s eyes went wide. “You—”

Just yesterday, Lyra had called and told them to take good care of her. Even if it was a girl, this would be the only daughter of the Cole family’s third generation. Sloane was lucky—carrying a girl meant Wren had taken notice.

Maren choked back her anger. “The Sir’s waiting for you in the dining room.”

Sloane was surprised.

She made her way to the dining room.

Jaxson was already eating. He glanced up as she entered. She wore a white knit tunic, the fabric stretched out of shape by her swollen body. Her steps were unsteady, her pace slow, her belly so heavy she looked like she’d carried multiple children before.

Sloane felt his eyes on her and consciously sat far from him. Then she heard his flat, cool voice. “Maren and the others have been with the Cole family for decades. You can’t expect them to cater to you in everything. You’re only pregnant. It’s not like you can’t move.”

Only pregnant?

Yeah.

To him, this accidental child probably meant nothing at all.

This sudden scolding of his had to be because Maren had been running her mouth to him.

And it wasn’t the first time.

Sloane stirred the porridge in her bowl, her voice even. “If they resent having to look after me, then send them back to the main house. I can manage on my own.”

After all, she cooked for herself, washed her own clothes, cleaned her own room. The staff only bothered putting on a show when Jaxson was around.

Jaxson’s brows drew together.

Sloane recognized that expression—it was his tell. Displeasure.

In work and in life, Jaxson was relentlessly controlling. He didn’t tolerate being contradicted.

“I’m telling you. I’m not asking for your input.”

Sloane lowered her head and fell silent.

Jaxson looked at her—that flat, hollow expression—and his jaw tightened.

He turned to Maren and the others and told them that from now on, she could handle her own affairs. They didn’t need to wait on her.

Sloane’s fingers tightened around her fork.

Breakfast ended.

Jaxson left.

Sloane went to Silverlake University.

She arrived at Leo’s office.

Behind the desk sat a young man in a tailored suit. His nose was sharp and straight, rimless glasses resting on its bridge, his bearing composed and deliberate.

Leo was only twenty-nine—the youngest full professor in Silverlake University’s Finance Department, a near-legendary figure whose name carried weight throughout the financial world.

Sloane raised her hand and knocked.

Chapter 3 Not a Good Match
When Leo looked up and saw the woman standing in the doorway, he froze for a beat. He didn’t recognize her at first—until she spoke.

“Professor Grant.”

Leo smoothed his expression without a trace and said, “You’re here.”

Sloane took off her mask and walked into the office.

“Professor Grant. Long time no see.”

Leo smiled gently. “Long time no see. I almost didn’t recognize you.”

Sloane hooked her lips in self-mockery. “With how I look now, I almost didn’t have the nerve to come see you.”

Leo stood and came around from behind the desk. “It’s normal for your figure to change during pregnancy. Once you have the baby, it’ll get better.”

“Sit.”

Sloane sat on the sofa.

Leo poured her a cup of warm water. “Warm up.”

Sloane took it. “Thank you.”

Leo glanced at her swollen belly. “How many months?”

“Twenty-five weeks,” Sloane said.

Leo said, “Then when school starts at the end of January next year, you’ll be right at your due date.”

Sloane pleaded, “I want to ask you for help, Professor. Can I delay enrollment?”

Having a baby was unavoidable, but she really didn’t want to miss this chance.

Leo’s face turned serious. “Why do you want to go?”

Sloane lowered her eyes. “After the baby is born, Jaxson is planning to divorce me. I don’t want to keep this twisted connection going either. I want to start over and live my own life.”

Six months wasn’t long. It wasn’t short. But for her, it felt as long as an entire lifetime.

Leo couldn’t help frowning. The sunny, lovable girl from back then had changed beyond recognition in such a short time. You could imagine what kind of torment—body and soul—she’d been through.

“I’m relieved you’ve thought it through and decided to pull yourself together,” he said. “You and Jaxson really aren’t a good match. From now on, you’ll definitely meet someone who truly loves you.”

Sloane kept her eyes lowered and nodded.

Back then, Leo had opposed her going to Jaxson’s side as his assistant. But she insisted. In the end, she crashed headfirst until she was bleeding.

She suddenly asked, “In your eyes, Professor Grant, what kind of person is Jaxson, really?”

Leo fell silent for a moment, then said slowly, “Someone who will do anything to reach his goals. Profit above everything else. He probably won’t have love.”

“Is that so?”

Yet the tenderness he showed that girl couldn’t be fake. Maybe only someone who loved to the point of ruin would lower himself like that.

Only a beautiful, stunning woman was worthy of him.

Sloane didn’t ask anything else.

“Since you’ve decided,” Leo said, “when the time comes, I can help you apply to delay enrollment.”

“Thank you, Professor.”

Leo had her fill out an application form.

Sloane finished filling it out.

“After the baby is born, will you leave her with the Cole family?” Leo suddenly asked.

Sloane tugged her lips helplessly. Even if she wanted to take the child, it would be impossible. She could only be the one who let this child down. “The Cole family should take good care of her.”

Leo didn’t press further. “I happen to need an assistant. Just for a month. Want to try?”

Sloane agreed without hesitation.

“Okay.”

Ever since she got pregnant, Jaxson’s side had transferred her to an insignificant position in the secretarial office. Overnight, she fell from CEO assistant to a nobody, and all her effort turned to foam.

She really did need a new job to distract herself, to make her life move again.

It would also be the perfect way to prepare in advance for further study later.

And she’d taken the day off anyway.
Sloane stayed on and began working as the professor's assistant. She had been Leo's student originally, and after those months of intense, high-pressure work at Jaxson's side—even though she'd spent the last few months in a fog—she still picked things up quickly. Handling the tasks came easily.

For the first time in a while, Sloane felt a flicker of clarity, like she'd found herself again—found the real value of her own existence.

Just like Leo always said, she was meant to thrive in a professional setting. Love was never supposed to be the only thing in life.

That night.

Jaxson didn't come home. Same as always—he only showed up once in a while.

Only this time, she didn't care anymore.

The next day.

She drafted her resignation letter ahead of time.

Jaxson oversaw the Cole Group's financial sector, including its banks and investment funds. In an industry soaked in betrayal and cutthroat ambition, where reputation and wealth were everything, the fact that he'd inherited the Cole family's core enterprises—and kept acquiring and expanding without pause—proved not only that he had an exceptional mind and ruthless instincts, but that he also possessed a cold, unyielding heart.

Sloane arrived at the office and happened to see Jaxson stepping out of his car.

Tall, broad-shouldered, dressed in a sharp suit—devastatingly handsome, commanding. Wealth and status only sharpened his appeal, giving him a mature, almost magnetic presence.

"Mr. Cole."

Employees lowered their heads in respect as he passed.

Sloane snapped out of it and quickly dipped her head too, stepping back a pace.

The man walked past as if she weren't there and strode into the building.

Sloane handed her resignation letter to Thea.

Thea was Jaxson's secretary.

She used to be Sloane's subordinate.

Funny how things turned out.

Now Sloane reported to her.

When Sloane had been abruptly demoted, the whole department had been stunned. Right after college, she'd been made the CEO's assistant.

That role demanded more than competence—appearance mattered too. And Sloane, whether in looks or figure, was unremarkable. Yet she'd still been chosen, which said something about her ability.

The CEO, notoriously hard to please, had even praised her more than once.

But Thea knew the real story.

Sloane was just a frog dreaming of swan meat—trying to sleep her way up. No matter how capable, she still wasn't decent.

That was exactly why.

Mr. Cole despised her down to his bones.

Thea glanced at the resignation letter, her eyes flicking over Sloane's pregnant belly. Her lips curled. "People should learn their place. Take a good look in the mirror. Don't think carrying a baby buys you a ticket up. Do you even know what kind of family the Coles are? What kind of standing you have?"

The fact that she and Jaxson were already legally married—no one in the company knew.

Chapter 4 I Don’t Want to Hear Your Excuses
“Have the financial report analysis for Vegas Partners done before lunch break ends.”

Sloane went back to her desk.

Even though she’d been transferred to the secretary department as nothing more than a low-level clerk, Thea still dumped a pile of work on her—tasks that were never supposed to be hers.

And Sloane accepted every single one.

She stayed at the company like this, working herself to the bone, but it was just her own self-deception. Jaxson was never going to spare her a second glance.

After finishing the report analysis, Sloane handed both the electronic file and the printed copy to Thea, then ordered delivery.

The company had a cafeteria, but she always brought her own lunch. She didn’t want to go somewhere crowded. She didn’t want people’s eyes weighing her up and down. She didn’t want to socialize. She only wanted to be alone, quiet, and undisturbed.

But she hadn’t prepared lunch this morning, so she made do with delivery.

While she waited.

A couple coworkers returned to the office after eating, walking in while chatting excitedly.

“Mr. Cole’s girlfriend is so young—she’s still at college, right?”

“Probably. She’s seriously gorgeous, like a doll.”

“And the way the CEO looked at her—so soft it was practically dripping. Who knew someone as stern as him could be that devoted? It’s literally the real-life romantic novels!”

The two of them talked as they came in, then noticed Sloane at her workstation, sitting there like a stone statue.

Ever since she’d been transferred to the secretary office, she barely spoke to anyone outside of work. Lately she’d gotten more and more withdrawn, wearing a mask all day like she couldn’t show her face.

It was hard to imagine that just over half a year ago, she’d been the CEO’s glorious, untouchable assistant.

After getting the delivery driver’s call, Sloane stood up.

When she went downstairs to pick up her food.

She happened to run into two hotel staff carrying boxed dishes, asking the front desk for directions. The receptionist swiped a card for the CEO’s private elevator.

Sloane saw the bottle of red wine in one staff member’s hand. Just that single bottle cost around two million dollars. Two million—pocket change to Jaxson, money he could earn in less than a minute.

She carried her delivered braised pork rice back upstairs.

At two in the afternoon.

Thea came to her and said, “Mr. Cole wants to see you.”

Sloane’s heart jumped. A vague, terrible premonition rose in her chest.

And sure enough.

The moment Sloane stepped into the CEO's office, the weight of the room pressed down on her like a physical force. She walked to the desk and said, "Mr. Cole."

When Jaxson looked up, his handsome face was cold and hard. Without a word, he hurled a file folder at her. It struck her square in the face.

The sharp edge of the paper sliced across her cheek. A sting flared instantly. She stared at the documents scattered at her feet—her report from this morning.

One hand braced against her stomach as she bent down awkwardly to gather them.

The man's dark eyes tracked the way she held her belly, the slow, careful way she crouched.

Sloane scanned the report in her hands and spotted several incorrect figures immediately. She said, "Mr. Cole, this isn't the report I wrote."

"Enough. I don't want to hear excuses."

Sloane's grip tightened on the papers until her knuckles went white.

Jaxson knew her capabilities. He wasn't refusing to listen—he was choosing to believe she'd failed.

To be hated this much by the man she loved... she was pathetic. A joke.

She drew a slow breath, closed her eyes for a moment, then opened them and forced the words out. "I kept a backup. I can send it to you now. After you've seen it, you can tear into me then. It won't be too late."

Jaxson's eyes narrowed. Displeasure flickered openly across his face.

Sloane's nerves pulled taut. Deep down, she was afraid of Jaxson—the kind of fear you have for someone with power, especially when his expression went cold. She almost never dared to contradict him.

But now she forced herself to stay steady. They were getting divorced anyway. She'd give him what he wanted. After this, she'd never set foot here again. She'd stopped hoping for anything from him.

So what was there to be afraid of?

"You think you've been wronged?" His voice was ice, edged with mockery.

Sloane met those sharp, black eyes. Her nails pressed into her palms as her voice came out heavier. "You didn't even ask what happened before you blamed me. Don't I deserve to defend myself?"

Jaxson's expression turned arctic. "Then that's something you deserve."

A violent pain ripped through Sloane's chest. The color drained from her face.

Then.

The lounge door opened.

A young girl stepped out in a pink satin slip dress. Her long black hair gleamed, her skin almost luminous, her features so delicate they were impossible to look away from.

“Jaxson!”

Her voice was like a gentle spring rain—soft, warm, and tender.

Sloane finally saw the girl’s face clearly. She really was stunning enough to make anyone feel inferior.

Sloane only looked once before the man barked harshly, “Get out!”

Sloane pulled her gaze back, swallowed the surge of emotion, turned around, and walked out.

The moment she left the office.

She heard the girl soothing him gently, and the man quickly calmed down.

Sloane lifted her chin, forcing the tears in her eyes back down.

She went to the deserted stairwell corner. One hand held the railing. Her emotions finally snapped, and tears fell in a steady stream. The pain in her heart twisted so hard her stomach churned.

To rip an eight-year love out of her heart completely was no different from carving bone and stripping flesh. But it was fine. Everything would get better. She would forget him completely.

She didn’t know how long passed.

When she finally calmed down and went back upstairs toward her workstation, she ran into the girl walking toward her. The girl was dressed head to toe in custom designer brands, exquisite from hair to heels—clearly someone raised in luxury and spoiled with love.

Adrian escorted her personally. He was Jaxson’s special assistant.

Seeing Sloane, the girl smiled and walked over, stopping in front of her. In a gentle voice, she said, “It’s okay now. Jaxson won’t blame you anymore.”

As she spoke.

She reached into her bag, took out a pearl, then took Sloane’s hand and placed it in her palm. “This is for you. Don’t be sad. And remember to treat the cut on your face. It won’t look good if a girl has a scar on her face.”

What a beautiful, kind girl.

Compared to someone glowing with youth like her, Sloane felt like a clown living in a dark world.

When Sloane didn’t respond at all.

Adrian frowned and reminded her coldly, “Aren’t you going to thank Miss Reed?”

So her last name was Reed.

Liora Reed withdrew her hand. “It’s fine. Let’s go.”

The two of them left.

Sloane stood where she was, staring at the silver-blue Australian white pearl in her palm—flawless, as pure as that girl.

She just didn’t know whether Miss Reed understood the fact that Jaxson was already married.

Back at her desk.

She printed the original document again and delivered it to Thea. When Thea saw her, there wasn’t a trace of shame on her face—only smug satisfaction.

“Did you see it clearly? That’s what a girl who’s worthy of the CEO looks like.”

Sloane slammed the materials down in front of her. “So I’m not worthy—and you’re not either. You can only pull trashy little tricks like this. You’ll never have a future in your life. You’re already in your thirties—hurry up and find someone to marry. Stop day dreaming.”

Chapter 5 Look Similar
Thea’s face changed in an instant. She slammed her palm on the desk and shot to her feet. “Sloane!”

Sloane couldn’t be bothered to respond. She turned and walked away.

Back at her workstation.

Sloane pulled out a small mirror and looked at the faint blood mark on one side of her cheek. It wasn’t deep. She wiped it once with a damp tissue. No need to do anything else. With a face like hers now, what did one more scar matter?

And then she thought of that girl again. Somehow, she looked familiar.

Near the end of the workday.

Sloane got a call from her dad. Ezra was back, and he wanted her home for dinner.

Sloane brightened. “Ezra is back? Didn’t you say he’d be home on the fifteenth?”

Her father said, “He wrapped up work and came back early.”

“Okay. I’ll come home as soon as I get off.”

Sloane drove back to the Powell family house.

Their place was in a mid-range complex in the west side of the city, a spacious secondhand condo they’d bought earlier this year.

Her father ran a mid-sized real estate company. They weren’t some elite dynasty, but they’d always lived comfortably, so Sloane had grown up in a well-off life.

But the market had turned cold. More than half a year ago, a failed investment blew a hole through the company’s finances, pushing it to the edge of bankruptcy. When her father found out she was pregnant with Jaxson’s child, he hadn’t forced her to march up to the Cole family and demand an answer.

Watching her father grow older and more worn by the day—so desperate he was already selling off assets just to pay debts—Sloane finally made her choice and went to the Cole family. Back then, she’d had her own selfish reasons. It wasn’t only for her father. It was for herself, too.

She did get what she wanted. The Powell family cleared the debt because of a huge bride price from the Cole family.

But she’d paid the price she was supposed to pay.

So the pain she suffered now… it was all her own doing. She couldn’t blame anyone else.

Back at the Powell House.

Nora came out of the kitchen. “Sloane, you’re back.”

When Sloane was nine, her mother divorced her father. Her mother took her brother and left Sloane behind.

Later, Nora met her father, but the two of them never got a marriage license. They lived together like partners.

At first, Sloane didn’t accept her—she even hated her. But little by little, she felt Nora’s kindness. And Ezra treated her so well. After losing her brother, she’d gained a new one.

“Aunt Nora, where are my dad and them?”

“They should be on the way. They’ll be back soon. Go rest for a bit first.”

“Okay.”

Sloane went back to her room. Even though she was married, her father had always kept a bedroom for her, renovated in the style she liked.

Back in a place that belonged to her, all the exhaustion and bitterness inside her vanished in a single breath.

She sat on the edge of the bed and saw the photo album on the nightstand. She reached for it and opened it. The very first photo was a torn family portrait.

The picture was old.

She had been eight that year.

Her young, handsome father held her in his arms. Beside him stood her brother—he’d been fourteen. On the other side was her mother.

She was the one who had ripped the photo.

Because she’d hated her mother for taking her brother and abandoning her and her dad. Time had passed, and now that ripping, splitting pain no longer existed the way it used to.

She turned to the next page.

In the photo, a teenage girl looked bright and beautiful. She wore a long white dress and a light-brown woven little square cap, standing beneath golden ginkgo trees. The sunlight fell perfectly over the girl’s radiant smile.

Long black hair. A small oval face. Features that were vivid and striking, moonlit and mesmerizing. Especially those eyes—sparkling like stars in the sky.

But later, she’d gotten seriously ill and had to take steroid medication. Her body slowly gained weight. No matter how she tried to lose it, nothing worked. She could only rely on starvation and exercise to keep herself from getting even bigger.

All at once, Sloane thought of the girl from today.

Her features looked somewhat like the girl in this photo—especially those eyes.

Chapter 6 Far Out of Her League
Knock, knock, knock.
"Sloane, your dad and brother are back," Nora called through the door after knocking.

Sloane didn't think much of it. She set the photo album down, got up, and walked out. The moment she saw the two men coming in, her face lit up. "Dad, Ezra."

Ezra and Silas Powell both looked at her.

"Sloane, I brought you something. Come see if you like it," Ezra said, motioning her over.

Sloane hurried toward him, delighted. "What is it?"

Ezra carried in several bags and set them on the coffee table. Then he pulled out a designer jewelry box and handed it to her. "Open it."

Sloane took it happily. Inside lay a beautifully crafted gold bracelet. "Thank you, Ezra. I love it."

"Glad you like it."

Ezra reached out and ruffled Sloane's hair with easy affection.

He'd also bought Nora a different gold bracelet that suited her, along with skincare sets for both women. For Silas, he brought tea and liquor, plus local specialties.

The atmosphere was warm, easy—the way home should feel.

Only here did Sloane feel like she could finally breathe.

"Sloane, when are you due?" Ezra asked, concern creeping into his voice.

Her belly really did look like someone else's late-term pregnancy.

"Two more months," Sloane answered.

"Sloane must be carrying a girl," Nora said with a smile.

Sloane nodded. "It is a girl."

"You checked?" Silas asked.

Nora seemed to catch something and tensed up alongside him.

"Yeah. But Wren cares a lot about this baby," Sloane said.

Silas finally let out a breath. "Good. As long as there's a child, you and Jaxson will slowly work things out down the road."

Sloane lowered her eyes. Her chest tightened, heavy and aching, and for a moment she didn't know how to respond. Jaxson had already brought up divorce.

But she couldn't hide it forever.

And she'd already decided to move out of Emerald Bay Mansion and come home.

Forget it. She'd tell them after dinner.

Nora prepared an elaborate meal.

Ezra had partnered with a friend to start a tech company. Two years ago, when the business was just getting off the ground, Silas hadn't hesitated—he'd given Ezra startup capital. The company was doing extremely well now, focusing mainly on AI. This trip had been for a partnership deal, and it had gone smoothly.

Silas, meanwhile, was in the process of selling off his own company.

Before, thanks to the bride price from the Cole family, the company had managed to stay afloat. But the economy was struggling now, and pivoting had proven nearly impossible. The business simply couldn't survive.

He was getting older, with far less energy than before. He believed strongly in Ezra's company. Ezra's company would enter its financing stage by the end of the year, so it was the perfect time to sell his own business and invest everything into Ezra's.

Then he shared another piece of good news: Silas was going to officially get the marriage license with Nora.

Nora's eyes immediately welled up.

Years of standing by his side had finally led to this.

Sloane had no objections. She knew her father had held back all these years because, deep down, he still missed her mother.

She'd never understood why her mother had divorced and left a man as good as him.

But now it didn't matter.

On a day like this—

She couldn't bear to ruin the mood.

But in the end, she still said it.

“Dad. Aunt Nora. Ezra.” She forced the words out. “Jaxson is planning to divorce me.”

The moment it left her mouth, the dining room went dead silent.

Everyone’s expression turned heavy, especially Silas. He lowered his head, his face tight.

The result wasn’t exactly a shock.

Only the speed of it was.

The Powell family and the Cole family had become in-laws, but there had been no wedding—just a marriage certificate. In the past six months, the two families had had no contact at all.

Jaxson had never once stepped into the Powell family home.

No matter the holidays, the Cole side never sent gifts.

Every time Sloane came home alone, Silas and Nora would prepare holiday gifts and have her deliver them to the Cole family.

When she brought them over, Wren would accept them politely, but Sloane knew she handed them straight to the staff at Cole Estate.

Lyra, on the other hand, had a servant throw them directly into the trash right in front of Sloane, telling her not to let her family send that kind of low-class junk again.

Jaxson only reminded her not to do something so pointless.

In a marriage that unequal, going their separate ways had always been a matter of time.

Sloane pressed her lips together and continued, “But we’ll wait until after the baby is born. And I already agreed to Professor Grant—I’m going to Stanford University for advanced study next February.”

Ezra was the first to break the suffocating silence. “Going for advanced study is good. Sloane, you’re so outstanding. You shouldn’t be trapped in a marriage. No matter what you decide, I’m backing you.”

Sloane smiled and nodded. “Thanks, Ezra.”

Silas sighed—a sigh full of endless helplessness and guilt. “Then divorce. It’s all Dad’s fault. People like us… ordinary folks… we really can’t reach a family like the Coles.”

Sloane’s eyes burned red. All the pain she’d endured lately suddenly felt small compared to this.

She had her family.

They were her shield, her support.

With them behind her, there was no hurdle she couldn’t get over.

Seeing her like that, Nora quickly grabbed a tissue and wiped at Sloane’s reddened eyes, soothing her.

In the end, the family still finished this dinner with smiles.

At the same time.

In the southern suburbs, at Cloud Peak One—an area that had existed for over twenty years, an old-money neighborhood with aging infrastructure.

A Bentley slowly stopped at the gate of Villa 12.

This villa was the one the Powell family had sold.

The car window slid down, revealing a handsome, flawless profile. He looked into the villa. Inside, the lights were blazing.

Warm yellow streetlight fell into his eyes, unable to hide the complexity and loneliness there.

He pulled his gaze back and lit a cigarette.

Then his phone vibrated.

He picked up and answered, his voice gentle. “What’s wrong, Liora?”

Liora’s sweetly complaining voice came through. “Declan, when are you getting here? I’m starving. And Jaxson won’t even let me eat first.”

Right after that, a low, indulgent male voice sounded on the other end. “Who was it that told me to remind her to watch her mouth? Now she’s blaming me?”

Liora huffed.

“If you’re hungry, eat first. I’ll be there soon,” he said.

He hung up.

Declan stubbed out the cigarette. Then, one last time, he looked out the window.

He raised the window and drove away from the villa.
