bodyText:
I told my best friend I had a new boy in my life.
Three days later, my cold, distant husband came home early from his business trip.
Suddenly, he was cooking for me, picking me up from work, and doing everything he could to make me happy.
One night, he pulled me into his arms and whispered, "Audrey, whatever he gives you, I can give you more. Just don't leave me."
I stared at him, completely confused.
Then he asked, his eyes red, "When are you going to let me meet him?"
I almost laughed.
Because the boy my husband was so jealous of wasn't another man.
And Nathan had absolutely no idea.

Marriage had become so predictable that I found myself looking for something to make life a little less dull.
So I got a new boy in my life.
Unfortunately, that sentence made its way to my contract husband.
After that, Nathan Reed, who had spent most of our marriage traveling for work, suddenly started coming home every day. He cooked for me, picked me up after work, and found increasingly creative ways to stay in my line of sight.
Then, at a charity gala, he looked at me with red-rimmed eyes and asked, “When are you going to introduce me to this new boy?”
“He’s young, obedient, and knows how to make you happy. Is that why you can’t let him go?”
I stared at him for two seconds.
“You really want to meet him?”
After Nathan said yes, I drove him out to the suburbs that same night.
That was where he finally met the “new boy” I had been keeping outside the city.
A six-month-old German Shepherd.
My marriage to Nathan began with two contracts.
One was the agreement between our families to jointly invest in a chain of rehabilitation clinics. The other was the prenuptial agreement we drafted for ourselves.
I was a corporate attorney, and Nathan ran a major hotel group. We had seen each other at the same family gatherings since we were young, knew each other’s names, and knew that the other had an impressive résumé. But we were never close.
When we got married, we put everything in writing: separate assets, work boundaries, boundaries involving our parents, and even what we would do if either of us fell in love with someone else and wanted to end the marriage peacefully.
At the time, I thought it was a good arrangement. Adults were better off putting risks on the table than relying on a few dramatic promises to hold a relationship together.
For the first six months of our marriage, things were polite and smooth.
Nathan flew from city to city overseeing new hotel openings, while I lived at my law firm, negotiating acquisitions and revising contracts for clients. When he left in the morning, I was usually still asleep. When I came home late at night, he might have just finished an overseas conference call.
Our housekeeper knew more about each other’s schedules than we did.
When Megan Foster heard that, she clicked her tongue dramatically.
“He’s handsome, rich, doesn’t check up on you, and doesn’t come home every day. Do you realize how many married women would consider that their ultimate dream husband?”
I turned another page in the due-diligence report in front of me.
“If you like him that much, I can give you his assistant’s email. You can try arranging his schedule for one week and see whether you can handle that blessing.”
“Stop changing the subject. Audrey Parker, your whole life is either the law firm or a client’s office. What’s the difference between being married and being single? Doesn’t it get boring?”
At that moment, spring rain was falling beyond the glass walls of the conference room, turning the city outside into a blur of gray and white. After spending an entire day staring at numbers, I had to admit that life did feel as though it was missing something alive.
That weekend, I went to a logistics park outside the city to inspect warehouse equipment for a client. On the way back, I came across a minor traffic accident.
Several cardboard boxes had overturned by the roadside. A small black-and-tan bundle rolled into the grass beside the road, its right hind leg scraped raw.
The puppy was trembling in terror, but when I reached toward him, he did his best to press his head into my palm. His wet nose brushed against my hand.
At the animal hospital, the veterinarian estimated that he was about four months old. He was a German Shepherd, had no microchip, and there was no way to identify his previous owner.
Our marital home was not suitable for a large dog. Nathan was particular about cleanliness, and I could not bring a dog into a home we shared without discussing it with him first.
So I settled the puppy in the small house on the outskirts of the city that my mother had left me. I asked a dog trainer I knew to check on him every day.
His ears had not fully stood up yet, and whenever he ran too fast, he looked like a black furry ball being carried by the wind. I named him Captain and recorded a video of him chasing his own tail.
When I left the house, I called Megan to share the news.
Music was blasting on her end, as though she were at a bar with friends.
“What did you say?” she shouted. “I can’t hear you. Hold on, I’m putting you on speaker.”
I raised my voice too.
“I said I have a new boy in my life!”
The noise on the other end went strangely quiet for two seconds.
Then Megan lowered her voice, nearly forcing the words through her teeth.
“Audrey Parker, do you know who I’m with right now?”
“No. Why?”
“Nathan Reed’s two childhood friends are here. Could you not say things like that unless you’re safely at home with the door closed?”
I glanced down at Captain, who was chewing on my shoelace, even more confused.
“I’m just talking about a dog. Why would I need to close the door?”
Someone called Megan’s name from across the room. She hung up in a hurry before I could ask what was going on.
Over the next few days, I ran into several acquaintances at a client’s celebration dinner. They would look at me for a little too long, then abruptly change the subject whenever I approached.
I was handling an equity acquisition worth several hundred million dollars at the time. I took dozens of calls a day and had no energy to figure out why everyone was acting so strangely.
Then, on Friday night, I came home after finishing a late shift and found the living room lights on.
Nathan was sitting on the couch, still wearing his trench coat. A suitcase from the airport rested by his feet.
He was not supposed to return from Singapore until the following week.
Instead, he sat there in silence, watching me with eyes dark enough to feel like a storm waiting to break.
“Did something go wrong with the project?” I asked, setting down my briefcase. “Or are you not feeling well?”
He did not answer the question.
“You’re surprised I came back early?”
“Of course. Yesterday, when we video-called, you said you were staying to oversee the final inspection.”
Nathan rose and walked toward me as though he wanted to confirm something from my expression. His jaw was tense, but his voice remained controlled.
“I left the rest to the vice president. I thought about it, and I realized I shouldn’t keep letting other people look after things at home for me.”
“What’s happening at home?”
He did not answer. Instead, he reached up and untied the scarf dampened by rain around my neck. His fingertips occasionally brushed my skin, carrying the coolness of someone who had just come in from outside.
I caught his wrist.
“Nathan, you’re acting very strange tonight.”
He looked at me for a long time.
Then he lowered his head and kissed me.
We were legally married, and our marriage had included a normal amount of intimacy. But Nathan had always been steady and restrained, even when he kissed me. Tonight, he kissed me as though he were trying to confirm that I still belonged somewhere within his reach. His breathing was uneven, and his arms tightened around me until I was pressed against the entryway cabinet.
I pushed at him, annoyed.
“I got caught in the rain. I’m damp.”
“I don’t care.”
“Well, I do. Let me change my shoes first.”
He paused. His forehead rested against mine before he finally loosened his arms.
“Audrey,” he said in a low, rough voice. “Who am I?”
The question was so absurd that I laughed.
“You were abroad for half a month and forgot your own name? Nathan Reed, my legally registered husband. Do you need me to find our marriage certificate?”
The darkness in his eyes eased for a moment, then settled again.
“Just remember that.”
That night, he was unusually clingy. As I drifted toward sleep, I vaguely heard him whisper against my ear.
“Don’t be so quick to replace me.”
The next morning, he was already dressed and taking a work call on the balcony.
I came out in my robe.
“You really aren’t going back to Singapore?”
“I’m not.” He ended the call and turned toward me. “The overseas project matters, but so does my marriage. I had the order wrong before.”
I paused, assuming that he had finally developed a married man’s sense of responsibility.
From that day on, Nathan began coming home with startling frequency.
One evening, I spent hours arguing over a compensation clause with opposing counsel. By the time the meeting ended, it was after nine. When I walked out of the building, Nathan’s car was waiting downstairs.
He opened the rear door and handed me a warm cup of soy milk.
“Did you eat dinner?”
I looked at my watch.
“Mr. Reed, you drove at least forty minutes from the east side of the city just to bring me soy milk?”
“I was nearby.”
His newest hotel was on the west side of the city.
The next day, I finished work early and came home to find him wearing an apron in the kitchen. His shirt sleeves were rolled to his elbows, and neatly chopped ingredients covered the counter.
I leaned against the doorway and looked him over seriously.
“Did you fire the chef?”
“No. I asked him to teach me two dishes.”
“Why?”
Nathan ladled soup into a bowl and pushed it toward me. His tone was calm, as though he were speaking at a board meeting.
“What’s outside may seem exciting for a while, but it isn’t necessarily clean or right for you. Home can be just as good, as long as you’re willing to spend time understanding it.”
I took a sip. The chicken soup was light and sweet, and it was unexpectedly good.
“You’re right,” I said, nodding. “When we aren’t busy, we should eat at home more often.”
Nathan stared at me as though he had thrown a punch into cotton. After a long pause, he managed a strained, “Okay.”
After dinner, Megan called me on video.
The moment her face appeared, she asked in a conspiratorial whisper, “Is your husband nearby?”
“He’s taking a shower. What is it?”
“How is the new boy? Has anyone found out?”
The mention of Captain immediately improved my mood.
“He’s doing great. He’s incredibly attached to me now. When I sit down to review a file, he lies at my feet. The second I reach out, he puts his head right into my hand so I can pet him.”
Megan sucked in a breath.
“You like them that obedient? I thought a tough corporate lawyer like you would prefer someone wilder.”
“He can be wild too. He has endless energy. The trainer said he dug up a whole patch of new grass in the yard today.”
“He’s young. Of course he has stamina,” Megan said, taking the conversation somewhere increasingly ridiculous. “Still, keep him hidden. Even if you and Nathan have a contract marriage, Nathan suddenly came back from overseas. He probably heard the rumors already.”
At that exact moment, the bathroom door opened.
Nathan emerged, drying his hair with a towel. Steam still clung to his shoulders and neck, and he had clearly heard the last line. He stopped at the foot of the bed, his gaze moving slowly from my face to the phone screen.
Megan saw him and ended the call in a panic.
I was about to explain that she always said strange things, but Nathan had already crossed the room.
He took my phone from my hand, placed it on the nightstand, then bent down and took my hand in his. Instead of speaking, he pressed his cheek into my palm and brushed against it lightly.
“You like it when someone puts his head into your hand on his own?” he asked.
The gesture was so unlike him that heat rushed to my ears.
“Were you listening to my call?”
“I only heard you say that you like someone young, energetic, obedient, and clingy.” The emotion he had been holding back finally cracked through his eyes. “Audrey, I can be obedient. I can stay with you every day. If you want something, you should at least tell me first instead of finding it outside.”
Before I could answer, he kissed me, as though he were afraid that one more word from me would be a rejection he could not bear to hear.
title: My Husband Auctioned Me to His Rival
